abstract: Nanoscale structure of the intercalated disk (ID) governs cardiac conduction through gap junctions and ephaptic interactions and is remodeled in arrhythmogenic disease. Computationally expensive models that resolve ID nanostructure have been confined to cables of tens of cells, such that the role of ID nanostructure on conduction has not been testable. Here, we show that a hybrid biophysical-neural network model removes this limit. A memory-based flow map, trained on finite element method (FEM) simulations of single junctions and short cables, defines surrogates that replace each junction in tissue. The hybrid model reproduces action potentials with 1-2 mV RMSE and conduction velocity restitution across multiple ID geometries with a mean error of 0.24%. Without retraining, surrogate models run in 2-D and 3-D tissues, with over one million junctions, 10^4-10^5 times faster than the FEM model and within an order of magnitude of a monodomain model that neglects ID structure. In large tissues with reduced gap-junctional coupling, regional cleft widening blocks conduction, whereas either change alone does not, linking ID remodeling to arrhythmogenic substrate.
